newsitem.title: CHINA: China imposes new punishments on dissident Wei.
newsitem.headline: China imposes new punishments on dissident Wei.

text.p: Prison authorities have accused China's best-known dissident, Wei Jingsheng, of fighting another inmate and imposed new punishments, a family member said on Thursday.

The veteran democracy activist who is serving a 14-year jail term for subversion blamed his deteriorating situation on the West's move to soften its stand on China's human rights record, said the relative, who visited him in mid-June at the Nanpu salt farm, a labour camp in the northern province of Hebei.

"The Chinese government feels the world environment has changed and the situation is to its advantage. The United States and other Western countries have succumbed and stopped criticising China," the relative quoted Wei as saying.
"China feels it can now do whatever it wants to me and other dissidents," Wei, 47, was quoted as saying.

China on Tuesday won Most Favoured Nation trade status for another year after members of the U.S. House of Representatives voted for the trading privileges despite opponents who criticised Beijing's human rights record.
Wei denied charges of brawling with other labour camp inmates, the relative said.

But prison authorities said they had testimonies from guards and inmates about the fight and had punished Wei by shutting off electricity to his cell and banning him from shopping at the prison canteen, said the family member who asked not to be identified.

"He can't buy medicinal liquor to ease his back pain... He can't store the food we bring him in the refrigerator because there is no electricity and he can't cook his own food," the relative told Reuters.
"We are worried about his health," the relative said. "We are also very worried about his situation... If something happens inside, they outnumber him and he will get the worse of it."
Prison officials could not be reached to comment.

Prison officials have accused Wei of kicking open the door to another inmate's cell and punching him after the inmate refused to lend Wei a screwdriver and grabbed the dissident by the collar, the relative said.
"He (Wei) believes the government is encouraging other inmates to pick a fight," the relative said.
Wei is regarded by many as the father of China's tiny, struggling democracy movement.

He was jailed in 1979 for "counter-revolutionary incitement", advocating democratic change and passing military secrets to a foreign reporter. He served all but the last six months of a 15-year jail term.
Wei was paroled in September 1993, detained again in April 1994 and sentenced to 14 years in prison in December 1995 on charges of conspiring to subvert the government.
A little-known European party fighting for human rights in China has nominated Wei for the 1997 Nobel Peace Prize. The winner will be announced in October.

In 1996, the European Parliament awarded Wei the Sakharov prize for freedom of thought. Its previous winners include South African President Nelson Mandela and Burmese opposition leader Aung San Suu Kyi -- both of whom later became peace laureates.
